editions.title: Microsoft Walks Away From Nscale Site as Neocloud Nerves Grow
editions.intro:
The biggest story of the day is Microsoft's reported withdrawal from an anchor deal for Nscale's first British data centre in Loughton, Essex. The Telegraph says Microsoft has pulled out weeks before the AI cloud startup's planned IPO, which is reported to seek up to $3bn. Nscale says it remains committed to the site and that its Microsoft relationship is strong, while Microsoft has not commented. Grid connection delays at the site were also reported, and the story is being read as a sign of wider caution toward neocloud firms.

That caution fed into a broader theme of AI-trade nerves. Bloomberg reports that a deepening selloff in US tech shares is exposing weak spots in Asia's AI supply chain, with rising financing costs threatening data-centre and hardware spending. The Financial Times, meanwhile, argues America's roughly $10tn AI infrastructure build-out is running into physical limits of power, equipment and money. Investors will look to Meta's earnings next, which the FT frames as a test of whether confidence in the AI spending boom can be restored.

Elsewhere, Ericsson beat expectations with third-quarter adjusted EBITA of SEK 10.1bn against a consensus of SEK 7.93bn, and its shares rose as much as 11% in Stockholm. On the chip front, a single unverified report says Nvidia wants Samsung, Micron and SK hynix to build custom HBM base dies on TSMC's 3nm process, while a separate rumour suggests China could let major firms buy H200 chips under tight caps. Both remain unconfirmed.

top_stories.title: Microsoft reportedly quits Nscale UK data centre before IPO
top_stories.summary: The Telegraph reports Microsoft has pulled out of anchoring Nscale's first British site in Loughton, Essex, weeks before an IPO seeking up to $3bn. Nscale says it remains committed and its Microsoft ties are strong, but Microsoft has not commented. The move adds to investor caution around neocloud firms.

top_stories.title: AI trade reversal hits Asia's picks-and-shovels stocks

top_stories.title: Ericsson beats expectations and shares jump
top_stories.summary: Ericsson posted Q3 adjusted EBITA of SEK 10.1bn versus about SEK 7.93bn expected, with 7% organic sales growth. Shares rose as much as 11%. It will merge its two Asian units from 1 January 2027 under new chief executive Per Narvinger.

top_stories.title: America's $10tn AI build-out meets physical limits
top_stories.summary: An FT analysis argues the AI infrastructure boom is colliding with real-world constraints on power, equipment and data-centre spending. It is a broad analytical piece rather than a single announcement, but it frames the funding debate.

top_stories.title: Can Meta's earnings restore AI boom confidence?
top_stories.summary: The FT's weekly preview asks whether Meta's coming results can revive faith in AI investment. Investors will watch closely given the scale of Meta's AI spending, though the analysis itself is not yet known.

top_stories.title: Nvidia reportedly standardises custom HBM base die on TSMC 3nm
top_stories.summary: A single unnamed report says Nvidia asked Samsung, Micron and SK hynix to make custom HBM base dies on TSMC's 3nm node, with Samsung reportedly accepting. The claimed gains are up to 30% more bandwidth and 15% less power, all unverified.

top_stories.summary: A Stocktwits item citing reports says Alibaba, ByteDance and DeepSeek could be allowed to buy H200 chips with tightly capped supply. It is unconfirmed and gives no official source or timeline.

editions.title: Nvidia RTX 5090 Row, TSMC Profit Record and Starlink Limits Dominate
editions.intro: TSMC posted a record quarterly profit, with demand for AI chips still far outstripping supply, but it signalled caution on 2027. Meanwhile, the AI trade showed strain: Asian chip suppliers were exposed to a US tech selloff, and reports that OpenAI's revenue trails expectations added to nerves. Ukraine's dispute with SpaceX over Starlink speed limits escalated, with Zelenskyy calling the restrictions deliberate. Apple's iPhone Duo faced shortages and Apple's chief executive called memory supply a crisis.

top_stories.title: TSMC records sixth straight record profit, cautious on 2027
top_stories.summary: TSMC reported record third-quarter net profit of NT$763.1bn, up 69%, with revenue up 51%. It guided to about 44% dollar revenue growth in 2026, but chairman C.C. Wei warned that price-sensitive consumer markets are under pressure and that the company is being prudent about 2027.

top_stories.title: Starshield speed limits cut Ukrainian interceptor drones
top_stories.summary: Speed limits on SpaceX's Starshield network reportedly cut links for interceptor drones above about 161 km/h, forcing Ukrainian units to cancel missions. Reports suggest the order came from the White House or was discussed by Musk and Trump, but these claims are unverified.

top_stories.title: Apple's Ternus calls memory shortage a crisis
top_stories.summary: Apple's chief executive told TIME that memory chip constraints are a crisis and all options should be considered. The comments follow a report that Apple tested memory chips from a Chinese firm, which prompted US warnings against them.

top_stories.title: Microsoft plans multi-gigawatt Maia 300 rollout
top_stories.summary: Microsoft plans to scale its Maia accelerators to multi-gigawatt deployments from 2027, with Maia 300 as its primary inference system. Analysts expect Maia to be only about 10% of its AI chip spend by early 2027, so Nvidia's position is not yet under threat.

top_stories.title: Intel confirms Razor Lake-AX timing and 700 TOPS target
top_stories.summary: Intel SVP Cho Min-sung confirmed Nova Lake for 2027 and Razor Lake-AX for 2028, the latter targeting 700 TOPS of AI compute. The aim is premium devices and physical AI.

top_stories.title: Tesla shows fan-powered Roadster, production 2028
top_stories.summary: Tesla demonstrated its next-generation Roadster using powered fans and a retractable rear wing for downforce. Musk said production begins in 2028, with reservations open at $50,000 for the base model and $250,000 for the Thrust trim.

rumour_watch.note: A reported $20bn revenue shortfall at OpenAI, relayed without a named source. Plausible given the market backdrop, but it is an internal figure and OpenAI has not confirmed it.
Nvidia's Jeff Fisher reportedly denied the RTX 5090 is discontinued, citing tight supply. Credible on the record, but retailer listings at inflated prices suggest supply is genuinely thin.
Reported FTC demands aimed at OpenAI and Anthropic. Only a feed summary, and the story stresses it is not a finding of wrongdoing, so treat as unconfirmed.
DeepSeek says its new Flash model beats larger rivals on agentic tasks. Weights are public, but independent benchmarks are still pending.

editions.title: Chip stocks extend slide as TSMC posts record profit and Apple's Duo sells out
editions.intro: Semiconductor shares suffered their longest losing streak since 2006, with the Philadelphia index down more than 12% in a week and short sellers pocketing an estimated $32bn. The mood was sharply different at TSMC, which reported a record quarterly profit but warned of caution on 2027. Apple's foldable iPhone Duo went on sale to strong demand, with delivery dates slipping into 2027.

top_stories.title: Chip stocks suffer longest losing streak since 2006
top_stories.summary: The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell over 12% in seven days and was on course for an eighth straight loss. Short sellers have made an estimated $32bn in paper gains, according to S3 Partners.

top_stories.title: TSMC records sixth straight profit but turns cautious on 2027
top_stories.summary: Third-quarter net profit hit a record NT$763.1bn, up 69%, and 2026 dollar revenue growth is guided to about 44%. Chairman C.C. Wei warned that consumer markets face pressure from rising component costs, while AI demand still outstrips supply.

top_stories.title: Apple launches iPhone Duo foldable from $1,999
top_stories.summary: The foldable has a 5.4-inch outer and 7.6-inch inner display, with Touch ID on the power button. Apple calls pre-order demand extraordinary, and online delivery estimates have slipped into late January.

top_stories.title: Dell sees memory shortage worsening into 2027
top_stories.summary: Michael Dell expects HBM and DRAM shortages to get worse next year, with supply constraints lasting up to four years. Dell holds a record $95bn of back-ordered AI and enterprise server orders.

top_stories.title: Eight US states sue OpenAI over ChatGPT harm to children
top_stories.summary: Attorneys general in eight states filed lawsuits on 14 October under consumer protection and public nuisance laws. They seek court-ordered changes to ChatGPT, civil penalties and a bar on developing self-improving models.

editions.title: Chip rout deepens as Tesla Roadster and iPhone Duo dominate
editions.intro: Semiconductor stocks extended a historic sell-off, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index on course for an eighth straight loss and short sellers reportedly up $32 billion. Big Tech logged its steepest weekly drop since the 'liberation day' sell-off as investors rotated into government debt. Meanwhile, Tesla unveiled its long-delayed Roadster with SpaceX technology, and Apple's foldable iPhone Duo sold out with deliveries pushed into 2027.

Finance.title: Oil spikes to $110 on Middle East escalation; AI jitters hit stocks
Finance.summary:
The biggest market move in the feed is oil. Brent crude jumped to a five-month high of $110 a barrel after reports of a new Middle East escalation, with Saudi Arabia-led forces said to have intercepted missiles aimed at energy hubs. The spike is set against a wider backdrop in which the Strait of Hormuz is reported closed and Brent is up sharply since the Gulf conflict began, pushing Central Asian producers to revive pipeline routes to Europe.

Equities are nervous. Reports describe accelerating US inflation, with CPI at 3.7% year on year, and turbulence in AI-linked shares, which has lifted options bets on a higher VIX. Analysts are split on whether the AI wobble is a passing jolt or a sign of a bubble, with debt-funded firms such as CoreWeave under particular scrutiny. Bank earnings and rising borrowing costs are also in focus.

In the UK, the Chancellor's first Budget on 28 October dominates the agenda. Reports point to a possible windfall tax on banks of roughly £7bn, while Healey has also been linked to changes to business rates and an Amazon crackdown. Pressure on the Bank of England is growing, with inflation at 3.1% and some commentators urging a rate rise, though GDP unexpectedly rose. Separately, Alberta's independence vote on 19 October is a political risk for Canadian oil.

points.text: Wall Street ended the week mixed as tech weakened and volatility rose; US CPI rose to 3.7% year on year.
Reports say Healey is weighing a roughly £7bn bank windfall tax ahead of the 28 October Budget; banks face share pressure.
Bailey is under pressure to act on rates as CPI sits at 3.1% and Bank rate is 3.75%.

Alberta votes on 19 October on a first step toward separation; the province sends about 90% of crude exports to the US.
China has proposed export controls on solar-manufacturing technologies, which could limit overseas transfer of know-how.

World.title: France's cost-of-living protests turn violent and spread across Europe
World.summary:
Saturday's nationwide protests in France, which began as student grievances over teacher absences and crumbling school buildings, widened into anger over living costs, fuel prices and police conduct. Interior ministry figures put attendance at 550,000, while the CGT union claimed 800,000. Clashes, arson and looting hit Paris, Marseille, Limoges and other cities, with about 1,800 arrests reported and a crisis government meeting due on Monday. Reports of damage to around 1,500 businesses point to losses in the hundreds of millions of euros, and the unrest is being framed as a warning ahead of next year's presidential election. Similar cost-of-living protests reached Milan, Lisbon, Belgium and Albania.

Energy is the second major thread. Attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, including reports of a super tanker ablaze after hitting a mine, and drone strikes on Russian and Ukrainian energy sites have pushed crude higher. Washington's decision to pause a sweeping package of Russia sanctions for 60 days has added uncertainty, with Rubio linking the move to energy price pressures from the Iran war and Houthi attacks. Ukraine's president has called the pause unfortunate and urged backing for the legislation.

For markets, the French unrest bears on the CAC 40 and European sentiment, while oil and tanker stocks are the most direct beneficiaries of the Gulf and Black Sea disruptions. Most other stories, from the Kenyan Ebola cases to the Alberta military base fire, carry little direct market relevance.

points.text: Zelenskyy urges backing for new US Russia sanctions after Trump signs a 60-day pause on the package.
IRGC says a super tanker caught fire after hitting a mine in the Strait of Hormuz; reports not independently verified.

Drone attacks on Black Sea shipping intensify, with a tanker ablaze off Romania and seven crew reported missing.
Czech opposition wins 22 of 27 contested Senate seats, leaving Babis's ANO with none.
At least 17 killed in a stampede at a Durga Puja gathering in north Kolkata, with 25 injured.

Tech.title: AI trade wobbles as funding costs and deal doubts mount
Tech.summary:
The dominant theme today is unease over the AI investment boom. Bloomberg reports a deepening selloff in US tech shares that is exposing weakness in Asia's AI supply chain, with rising financing costs threatening the data-centre and hardware spending that has powered picks-and-shovels suppliers. The Financial Times describes America's roughly $10tn AI infrastructure build-out as running into the hard economics of the physical world, while SemiAnalysis argues that more than 300 local data-centre moratoriums have delayed only a small share of projects.

Neocloud and infrastructure names are feeling the strain most directly. The Telegraph reports, unconfirmed, that Microsoft has pulled out of a UK data-centre anchor deal with Nscale, weeks before the British AI cloud firm's planned IPO. Nscale says it remains committed to the site. Separately, reports of a possible Microsoft-linked Texas power plant and a rumoured OpenAI revenue shortfall of about $20bn add to the sense of scrutiny over who pays for AI capacity. Meta's earnings, previewed by the FT as a test of confidence in the AI boom, will be closely watched.

Chips and hardware remain the centre of news flow. Nvidia is reportedly asking Samsung, Micron and SK hynix to build custom memory base dies on TSMC's 3nm process, while Microsoft's Maia 300 plan signals a push into in-house silicon. Apple's foldable iPhone Duo dominates consumer tech coverage, with reports of supply constraints and Apple's chief executive calling memory shortages a crisis. Most of these items are rumours or single-source reports, so readers should weigh them accordingly.

points.text: Microsoft reportedly quit Nscale's Loughton data-centre deal; Nscale says it stays committed and the site faces grid delays.
Bloomberg's Gurman calls Apple's global iPhone Duo pre-order rollout a major mistake, with shipping dates slipping to around January.
Apple's John Ternus tells TIME memory chip supply is a crisis and defends using Google Gemini in the new Siri.
Ericsson beat expectations with Q3 adjusted EBITA of SEK 10.1bn and 7% organic growth; shares rose as much as 11%.
Unconfirmed reports say China could let Alibaba, ByteDance and DeepSeek buy Nvidia H200 chips, with tightly capped supply.
Anthropic is lobbying for a federal AI safety bill that would only allow blocking releases above $1bn damages or 50 casualties.

Fashion.title: Chanel expands in China as luxury rethinks its market
Fashion.summary:
The most significant story today is Chanel's plan to open its first Wuhan boutique at the SKP department store. Based on user posts on Xiaohongshu, Chanel has unveiled a stand-alone store hoarding on K Avenue, a 1.5 km pedestrian promenade that will eventually host around 40 stand-alone stores, positioned between Louis Vuitton and Cartier. The store would be Chanel's second in the Hubei city region and its 13th boutique in China. Celine, Giorgio Armani and Prada are also set to open at SKP Wuhan, timed to coincide with the WWD x SKP Global Fashion & Beauty Summit.

The move reflects how luxury brands in China are adjusting to a prolonged market reset, closing weak stores while testing new regional markets. Expansion in a second-tier city such as Wuhan, clustered alongside peers, suggests that brands are still willing to invest in China, but with a more selective footprint than in earlier years.

Elsewhere, the Business of Fashion flagged that the United States, a key source of demand for luxury goods, may be losing momentum. The feed item is only a headline, so the scale and causes of any slowdown are unclear. Victoria's Secret's Pink is also in focus, taking the halftime slot at the Victoria's Secret fashion show. Pink reported high-single-digit comparable sales growth in Q2, its fifth consecutive quarter of growth, and is trying to rebuild its apparel business.

points.text: Pink takes the halftime slot at the Victoria's Secret fashion show, livestreamed on YouTube, as the sub-brand targets 18 to 24-year-olds.
Pink reported high-single-digit comparable sales growth in Q2, its fifth straight quarter of growth, and launched its Marshmallow bra.
